sections.heading: Interstates, weather, distraction and defensive driving
sections.markdown:
## C2 — Interstates, weather, distraction and defensive driving

FACT_ID: sec13-R01 | anchor: A71
If stranded in a blizzard, stay calm and remain with the vehicle. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R02 | anchor: A71
For a stranded vehicle, crack a window for ventilation and use the engine and heater sparingly only with ventilation and a snow-free exhaust pipe. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R03 | anchor: A71
Use hazard flashers to help work crews see a stranded vehicle and use its interior lamp at night. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R04 | anchor: A71
If several people are stranded together, alternate sleeping and keeping watch. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R05 | anchor: A71
If wheels drop off pavement, grip the steering wheel firmly and straddle the edge instead of immediately turning back. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R06 | anchor: A71
After an edge drop, reduce speed, check traffic and return gradually to the driving lane when safe. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R07 | anchor: A71
Visual distraction takes the eyes away, manual distraction takes the hands away and cognitive distraction takes attention away from driving. [A71]
Source: [A71 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec13-R08 | anchor: A72
Text messaging can involve visual, manual and cognitive distraction together. [A72] [A71]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R09 | anchor: A72
The handbook lists a texting-and-driving fine range of two hundred to five hundred dollars. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R10 | anchor: A72
A hands-free phone conversation can still distract the driver. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R11 | anchor: A72
Eating, reading, handling clothing, reaching to the floor, grooming or changing media can distract a driver. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R12 | anchor: A72
Children, other passengers and pets can distract the driver. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R13 | anchor: A72
Secure children properly, keep them occupied appropriately and pull over safely if they need attention rather than tending to them while moving. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R14 | anchor: A72
Keep passenger behavior under control and reserve arguments or upsetting conversations for a safe place outside the driving task. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R15 | anchor: A72
Secure pets in an appropriate carrier, kennel or harness and do not allow a pet on the driver's lap. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R16 | anchor: A72
Entering navigation destinations, searching for radio content or adjusting climate controls can distract from vehicle control. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R17 | anchor: A72
Using portable-device internet or email while driving adds distraction and crash risk. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec13-R18 | anchor: A73
Set the seat, mirrors, climate and radio controls before beginning to drive. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R19 | anchor: A73
Check messages before driving and ask passengers to operate navigation, radio or climate controls when help is needed. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R20 | anchor: A73
The manual suggests using normal stops for vehicle-control adjustments. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R21 | anchor: A73
The printed noncommercial rule prohibits handheld wireless use to read, type or send written messages while operating a motor vehicle. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R22 | anchor: A73
The manual prohibits operating a vehicle on a public road with a television screen visible to the driver. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R23 | anchor: A73
Watching crash scenes, police stops, construction, advertising, scenery or address details can draw attention away from driving. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R24 | anchor: A73
Aggressive driving includes frightening or rude behavior such as tailgating, cutting off vehicles, running red lights or failing to yield. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R25 | anchor: A73
Avoid driving while angry or upset and treat other road users courteously. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R26 | anchor: A73
Begin a trip rested; if drowsy, stop driving and pull over safely for rest. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R27 | anchor: A73
The handbook describes a short ten-to-twenty-minute nap as a fatigue-rest option. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R28 | anchor: A73
The fatigue tips suggest a midafternoon break and avoiding early-morning or late-night driving. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec13-R29 | anchor: A74
Fatigue warnings include heavy eyelids, yawning, head nodding, missed signs, poor memory of recent miles and unintended lane departures. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R30 | anchor: A74
The handbook mentions changing drivers as one response to fatigue. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R31 | anchor: A74
The manual says an open window, chewing gum or loud radio does not prevent drowsiness and that caffeine or energy drinks are unreliable for alertness. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R32 | anchor: A74
Do not use phone calls or texting as a way to stay awake while driving. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R33 | anchor: A74
Defensive driving means staying alert to prevent crashes. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R34 | anchor: A74
The handbook describes a look-ahead planning interval of at least ten to fifteen seconds. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R35 | anchor: A74
Look to both sides where road users could cross, and check both directions at an intersection even after the signal changes. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R36 | anchor: A74
Check rear traffic at least every ten seconds and when changing lanes, backing, slowing or descending steep hills. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R37 | anchor: A74
A shoulder glance checks the blind area beside the vehicle that mirrors do not show. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R38 | anchor: A74
Signal at least one hundred feet before a planned direction change, including lane changes, turns, freeway entry or leaving a curb. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R39 | anchor: A74
Use headlights when other vehicles are hard to see and whenever the windshield wipers are used. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R40 | anchor: A74
A sharp horn blast can warn of an immediate collision danger; brief brake taps can warn following drivers of slowing. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R41 | anchor: A74
Maintain a space cushion around the vehicle to allow time to react, stop or pass safely. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R42 | anchor: A74
To check following space, time the gap from a fixed roadside marker; reaching it in less than three seconds is too close, and adversity calls for a longer gap. [A74] [A75]
Source: [A74 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec13-R43 | anchor: A75
The handbook treats three seconds as a following-distance minimum and adds one second for each adverse factor, such as rain or heavy traffic. [A75] [A74]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec13-R44 | anchor: A75
Keep lateral space from oncoming traffic and parked vehicles, and protect rear space through steady speed and advance slowing signals. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]
